Because only the hydrogen on the unsubstituted side can be anti-periplanar to the axial bromide
quiz.why: E2 demands anti-periplanar geometry, which on this ring is only satisfied by one specific hydrogen, overriding Zaitsev preference. Bromide is a good leaving group, the substrate is secondary, and an E1 pathway would follow Zaitsev instead.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best leaving group in a substitution reaction?
quiz.why: Good leaving groups are weak bases, and tosylate is the resonance-stabilized conjugate base of a very strong acid. Hydroxide, amide and fluoride are all strong or hard bases and leave poorly.

quiz.q: Which reagent converts 2-propanol to acetone?
quiz.why: A secondary alcohol oxidizes to a ketone and stops there, and chromic acid accomplishes this. LiAlH4 and NaBH4 are reducing agents, and PBr3 simply replaces the OH with bromide.

quiz.q: An ethyl ester is treated with excess LiAlH4 and then water. What is the major product?
quiz.why: LiAlH4 reduces esters all the way down to the primary alcohol, passing through an aldehyde that is reduced immediately. NaBH4 is the reagent that would leave the ester alone, and reduction never produces an acid.

quiz.q: 2-methyl-1,2-epoxypropane reacts with sodium methoxide in methanol. At which carbon does methoxide attack?
choices: Neither carbon; the epoxide is inert
quiz.why: Under basic conditions the reaction is SN2-like and sterics dominate, so attack occurs at the least hindered carbon. Attack at the more substituted carbon would require acid to protonate the epoxide first, and epoxides are far from inert because of ring strain.

quiz.q: You need to make cyclohexyl methyl ether by Williamson synthesis. Which combination works best?
quiz.why: Williamson is SN2, so the halide must be unhindered; methyl iodide is ideal and the secondary cyclohexyl group belongs on the alkoxide. Using cyclohexyl bromide with a strong alkoxide base favors E2 elimination instead.

quiz.q: Which ring is antiaromatic rather than aromatic?
choices: Cyclobutadiene, a planar cyclic ring with 4 pi electrons
The cyclopentadienyl anion, with 6 pi electrons
quiz.why: Four pi electrons fits 4n, the antiaromatic count, and makes cyclobutadiene markedly unstable. The other three all have the 4n+2 count of 6 and are aromatic.

quiz.q: Why is aniline a far weaker base than cyclohexylamine?
choices: Aniline has no lone pair on nitrogen
Aniline's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring and is less available
Aniline is sterically hindered by the ring
Aniline is already protonated at neutral pH
quiz.why: Resonance donation into the ring ties up the nitrogen lone pair, dropping the conjugate acid pKa to about 4.6 versus 10.6 for an alkylamine. The lone pair exists but is delocalized, and sterics are a minor effect here.

quiz.q: Nitrobenzene reacts far more slowly than benzene in bromination, and bromine enters the meta position. Why?
choices: The nitro group blocks ortho and para sterically
The nitro group is an ortho-para director that is overwhelmed by sterics
The nitro group withdraws electron density and destabilizes the ortho and para arenium ions most
quiz.why: Attack ortho or para places positive charge directly on the carbon bearing the electron-poor nitro group, which is prohibitive, so meta is the least bad option and the whole ring is deactivated. Sterics are not the driver, and nitrobenzene remains fully aromatic.

quiz.q: Which carboxylic acid derivative is the most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
quiz.why: Chloride is the weakest base and therefore the best leaving group, and it donates almost nothing back into the carbonyl. Amides sit at the opposite end because nitrogen donates strongly and the amide anion is a terrible leaving group.

quiz.q: A patient is given enalapril, which has no ACE-inhibiting activity in the test tube yet lowers blood pressure. What chemistry explains this?
choices: Liver esterases hydrolyze the ester to release active enalaprilat
Gastric acid oxidizes it to the active form
The amide bond is reduced in plasma
It is a racemate that resolves in vivo
quiz.why: Enalapril is an ester prodrug cleaved by hepatic esterases to the active diacid. Amides resist plasma hydrolysis and are not reduced in the body, and no oxidation or resolution step is involved.

quiz.q: An IR spectrum shows a strong sharp band at 1735 wavenumbers and no absorption above 3100. Which compound fits?
quiz.why: An ester C=O lands near 1735 and an ester has no O-H or N-H to absorb above 3100. An alcohol and an acid would both show broad O-H bands, and an alkene has no strong carbonyl band.

quiz.q: A proton NMR shows a 6-hydrogen doublet near 1.2 ppm and a 1-hydrogen septet near 3.9 ppm. Which fragment is present?
choices: An isopropyl group attached to oxygen
quiz.why: Two equivalent methyls split by one neighbor give a 6H doublet, and that single CH split by six neighbors gives a septet, shifted downfield to 3.9 by an attached oxygen. An ethyl group gives a triplet and quartet, tert-butyl gives a 9H singlet, and aromatic hydrogens appear near 7 ppm.

quiz.q: A mass spectrum shows peaks at m/z 108 and 110 of nearly equal intensity. What does this indicate?
quiz.why: Bromine's two isotopes are almost equally abundant, so M+ and M+2 are nearly equal in height. Chlorine gives an M+2 about one third the height of M+, and nitrogen shifts the molecular ion to an odd mass rather than creating an M+2 doublet.

quiz.q: At physiologic pH of 7.4, glycine exists predominantly as which species?
choices: A zwitterion with a protonated amine and a deprotonated carboxylate
Fully neutral with both groups uncharged
quiz.why: The carboxyl pKa near 2 is well below 7.4 so it is deprotonated, while the amine pKa near 9.5 is above 7.4 so it stays protonated. The fully neutral form is never significantly populated in water.

scenarios.title: Exam problem: assign configuration, then choose a mechanism
scenarios.intro:
A midterm hands you 2-bromobutane drawn with a wedge-dash structure at carbon 2. Part A asks you to assign R or S. Part B puts the same compound in two different flasks with two different reagents and asks what comes out of each. Work it the way a grader wants to see it.

> **Key:** Assign configuration before you touch the mechanism. The stereochemical answer depends on which mechanism runs.

steps.prompt: Carbon 2 of 2-bromobutane bears four groups: `Br`, `CH3`, `CH2CH3`, and `H`. What is your first move in assigning R or S?

choices.text: Rank the four groups by the atomic number of the atom directly attached
choices.feedback: Correct. CIP always starts at the first atom out. Bromine at atomic number 35 wins immediately; hydrogen at 1 is last.

choices.text: Rank by the size of the whole group, so the ethyl beats the bromine
choices.feedback: No. CIP uses atomic number at the first point of difference, not molecular size or mass of the group. Bromine outranks any carbon chain.

choices.text: Look up whether the compound rotates light clockwise
choices.feedback: Optical rotation is measured, never predicted. R/S and plus/minus are independent labels, so this tells you nothing about configuration.

choices.text: Count the stereocenters first to see how many assignments are needed
choices.feedback: Reasonable bookkeeping, and there is exactly one stereocenter here, but you still have to rank the groups before you can assign anything.

steps.prompt: You have `Br` as priority 1 and `H` as priority 4. Now you must break the tie between `CH2CH3` and `CH3`, both of which start with carbon. How?

choices.text: The methyl wins because it is simpler
choices.feedback: No. Simplicity has no role in CIP. You must compare the sets of atoms one bond farther out.

choices.text: Move one bond outward and compare the attached atom sets: ethyl is (C,H,H) and methyl is (H,H,H), so ethyl wins
choices.feedback: Exactly right. At the first point of difference, carbon beats hydrogen, so ethyl is priority 2 and methyl is priority 3.

choices.text: Add up the total atomic mass of each group and take the heavier one
choices.feedback: This happens to give the right answer here but it is the wrong rule and will fail you elsewhere. CIP compares atom sets outward in order, never summed mass.

choices.text: Declare it a tie, so the center is not a stereocenter
choices.feedback: Ethyl and methyl are genuinely different groups, so this is a real stereocenter. A true tie, such as two methyls, is what would kill the stereocenter.

steps.prompt: The hydrogen is drawn on a **wedge**, pointing toward you. Tracing `Br` to ethyl to methyl reads clockwise as drawn. What is the configuration?

choices.text: R, because clockwise is R
choices.feedback: This is the classic trap. Clockwise means R only when the lowest priority group points away from you. Here it points toward you, so the reading must be reversed.

choices.text: S, because the lowest priority group faces you so the apparent direction is reversed
choices.feedback: Correct. With priority 4 on a wedge, read the direction as drawn and then flip it: apparent clockwise means the true assignment is S.

choices.text: Cannot be determined without a model kit
choices.feedback: You can always determine it on paper. The reversal rule for a wedge-drawn lowest priority group exists precisely so you do not need a model.

choices.text: Meso, because there is a mirror plane
choices.feedback: Meso requires at least two stereocenters that cancel. There is only one here, so the molecule is simply chiral.

steps.prompt: Part B, flask one: (S)-2-bromobutane is dissolved in **acetone** with **sodium iodide**. Predict the outcome before predicting the stereochemistry.

choices.text: SN1, because the carbocation is stabilized by acetone
choices.feedback: Acetone is polar aprotic and does a poor job stabilizing cations, and a secondary halide with a strong nucleophile present does not need to ionize. SN1 is not the pathway here.

choices.text: E2, because iodide is a strong base
choices.feedback: Iodide is a strong nucleophile but a very weak base, since HI has a pKa near minus 10. Weak bases do not drive E2.

choices.text: SN2, because iodide is a strong nucleophile and weak base in a polar aprotic solvent on a secondary substrate
choices.feedback: Correct. Every factor points the same direction, and the product is 2-iodobutane with inverted configuration at the stereocenter.

choices.text: No reaction, because iodide is a worse leaving group than bromide
choices.feedback: Leaving group ability governs the group departing, not the one attacking. Iodide is both a great nucleophile and a great leaving group, which is what makes this substitution reversible in principle but driven by NaBr precipitating from acetone.

steps.prompt: Flask two: the same (S)-2-bromobutane is heated with **sodium ethoxide in ethanol**. What is the major product?

choices.text: 2-ethoxybutane by SN2
choices.feedback: Ethoxide can do SN2, but on a secondary substrate with heat, its strong basicity wins and elimination dominates. Substitution here is a minor product.

choices.text: 1-butene, the Hofmann product
choices.feedback: Ethoxide is a small base, not a bulky one, so it has no trouble reaching the interior proton. Hofmann product requires something like potassium tert-butoxide.

choices.text: 2-butene, the Zaitsev product, by E2
choices.feedback: Correct. Strong small base plus secondary substrate plus heat equals E2, and Zaitsev favors the more substituted internal alkene.

choices.text: Racemic 2-butanol by SN1
choices.feedback: SN1 needs a weak nucleophile and a tertiary substrate; a strong alkoxide base on a secondary center does not go that route, and no water is present to give an alcohol.

steps.prompt: The grader asks one last thing: if you had started with **racemic** 2-bromobutane in flask one instead of pure (S), what would the product mixture look like?

choices.text: A racemic mixture of 2-iodobutane, because each enantiomer inverts to the opposite one
choices.feedback: Correct. SN2 inverts every molecule faithfully, but inverting a 50:50 input still gives a 50:50 output. Stereospecific is not the same as enantioenriched.

choices.text: A single enantiomer of 2-iodobutane, because SN2 always inverts
choices.feedback: Inversion is faithful per molecule, but you cannot create optical purity from a racemic starting material without a chiral reagent or a separation step.

choices.text: A racemic mixture, because the carbocation is attacked from both faces
choices.feedback: Right answer, wrong reason. There is no carbocation in an SN2 reaction; the racemic product simply mirrors the racemic input.

choices.text: Mostly 2-butene, because racemic mixtures favor elimination
choices.feedback: Stereochemistry of the starting material has no bearing on the substitution versus elimination balance. That is decided by substrate, base strength, solvent and temperature.

scenarios.debrief:
Two separate skills got tested here and they are graded separately. First, CIP assignment: rank by atomic number, break ties one bond outward, and reverse your reading whenever the lowest priority group points toward you. That reversal is the single most common lost point on stereochemistry questions.

Second, mechanism selection. Read the attacking species before anything else. A strong nucleophile that is a weak base, such as iodide, azide or cyanide, means substitution. A strong base, such as ethoxide or hydroxide, means elimination, and heat makes that more certain. Then let substrate class, solvent and sterics fine-tune the answer.

> **Trap:** A stereospecific reaction preserves the information in the starting material. It does not create new optical purity. Racemic in means racemic out.

scenarios.title: Exam problem: deduce a structure from spectra, then design its synthesis
scenarios.intro: The final exam gives you an unknown with molecular formula `C8H8O2`. You get a mass spectrum, an IR trace, and a proton NMR with integrations. The second half of the problem asks you to propose a two-step synthesis of the compound from benzene. Work the data before you guess.

steps.prompt: Start with the formula `C8H8O2`. What should you calculate first, and what does it tell you?

choices.text: Degrees of unsaturation: (16 + 2 - 8)/2 equals 5, so there is a benzene ring plus one more pi bond
choices.feedback: Correct. Four degrees accounts for a benzene ring and its three pi bonds, and the fifth is almost certainly a carbonyl given the two oxygens.

choices.text: Degrees of unsaturation, counting the oxygens, giving 7
choices.feedback: Oxygen never enters the degrees of unsaturation formula, because adding an oxygen into a chain does not change the hydrogen count. The correct value is 5.

choices.text: Molecular weight, so you can match the M+ peak
choices.feedback: Useful confirmation, and 136 will match the M+ peak, but the degrees of unsaturation is what actually narrows the structure.

choices.text: The number of NMR signals, since that is the most informative number
choices.feedback: You cannot count signals until you see the spectrum, and the formula-based calculation costs nothing and comes first.

steps.prompt: The IR shows a strong sharp band at **1720 wavenumbers**, a weak band just below 3000, and **nothing broad above 3000**. What does that rule in and out?

choices.text: A carboxylic acid, because 1720 is the acid carbonyl
choices.feedback: The carbonyl position fits, but a carboxylic acid always brings an enormous broad O-H from about 2500 to 3300. Its absence rules the acid out.

choices.text: An alcohol, because the band below 3000 is the O-H
choices.feedback: That band below 3000 is ordinary C-H stretching. An alcohol O-H is broad and sits at 3200 to 3600, and it is absent.

choices.text: A carbonyl is present, and the absence of any broad band above 3000 rules out both alcohol and carboxylic acid
choices.feedback: Exactly. With two oxygens, a carbonyl, and no O-H, the remaining candidate is an ester. That is the key deduction of the whole problem.

choices.text: An alkene, because 1720 could be a C=C stretch
choices.feedback: C=C absorbs weakly near 1650, not strongly at 1720. A strong sharp band in the 1700 to 1750 window is a carbonyl.

steps.prompt: The proton NMR shows exactly two signals: a **3-hydrogen singlet at 2.3 ppm** and a **5-hydrogen multiplet at 7.2 to 7.4 ppm**. Interpret both.

choices.text: A methyl with no neighbors next to a carbonyl, and a monosubstituted benzene ring
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. A singlet means zero adjacent hydrogens, 2.3 ppm places the methyl alpha to a carbonyl, and a 5H aromatic multiplet means one ring substituent.

choices.text: An ethyl group and a disubstituted ring
choices.feedback: An ethyl group would show a triplet and a quartet totaling five hydrogens, and a disubstituted ring shows four aromatic hydrogens, not five.

choices.text: A methyl on the ring itself, since 2.3 ppm is the tolyl methyl range
choices.feedback: A tolyl methyl does appear near 2.3, so this is a genuinely tempting read, but it would leave the ring disubstituted and only four aromatic hydrogens. The 5H integration says the ring carries exactly one group.

choices.text: An aldehyde hydrogen and a benzene ring
choices.feedback: An aldehyde hydrogen appears as a 1-hydrogen signal at 9 to 10 ppm. Nothing in that region was reported.

steps.prompt: Put it together. `C8H8O2`, an ester, a `CH3` with no neighbors sitting next to a carbonyl, and a monosubstituted benzene. Which structure fits?

choices.text: Methyl benzoate, `C6H5-CO-O-CH3`
choices.feedback: The formula fits, but a methyl on the ester oxygen appears near 3.9 ppm, not 2.3. The observed shift says the methyl is attached to the carbonyl carbon, not to oxygen.

choices.text: Phenyl acetate, `CH3-CO-O-C6H5`, an acetate ester of phenol
choices.feedback: Correct. The acetyl methyl lands at 2.3 ppm as a singlet, and the phenyl group on the ester oxygen gives five aromatic hydrogens. This is the same acetyl-on-phenol motif found in aspirin.

choices.text: Phenylacetic acid, `C6H5-CH2-COOH`
choices.feedback: This would show a broad acid O-H in the IR and a 2-hydrogen benzylic singlet, not a 3-hydrogen one. The IR already ruled out the acid.

choices.text: Acetophenone, `C6H5-CO-CH3`
choices.feedback: Acetophenone matches the NMR nicely but its formula is C8H8O, with only one oxygen. You need to account for both oxygens in C8H8O2.

steps.prompt: Second half of the problem: propose a synthesis of phenyl acetate **from benzene**. What is your first step?

choices.text: Friedel-Crafts acylation with acetyl chloride and AlCl3
choices.feedback: That builds acetophenone, a ketone with the acetyl group bonded to a ring carbon. You need the acetyl bonded through an oxygen instead.

choices.text: Install an oxygen on the ring to make phenol, for example by sulfonation then alkali fusion, or by nitration, reduction and diazotization followed by hydrolysis
choices.feedback: Correct approach. Benzene has no oxygen, so you must install the phenol OH first; either classical route gets you there.

choices.text: Brominate the ring with Br2 and FeBr3
choices.feedback: This installs a halogen, which is a reasonable handle in some routes, but it is not a path to a phenol under ordinary conditions and adds steps.

choices.text: Oxidize benzene directly with KMnO4 to get phenol
choices.feedback: Benzene resists direct oxidation because aromatic stability protects the ring. Permanganate oxidizes alkyl side chains, not the ring itself.

steps.prompt: You now have phenol in hand. How do you finish the synthesis of phenyl acetate, and why choose that reagent?

choices.text: Treat phenol with acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride, because a reactive derivative converts readily into the less reactive ester
choices.feedback: Correct. You may always move down the reactivity ladder: acid chloride or anhydride to ester. This is exactly how aspirin is made industrially, from salicylic acid plus acetic anhydride.

choices.text: Treat phenol with acetamide, since amides transfer acyl groups easily
choices.feedback: Backwards. Amides are the least reactive derivative, so an amide will not acylate an alcohol. You can go from amide-precursors down to amides, never up.

choices.text: Treat phenol with acetic acid and a trace of sulfuric acid under Fischer conditions
choices.feedback: This is a real reaction but a poor choice. Fischer esterification is an equilibrium and phenols are weak nucleophiles, so yields are low. An anhydride drives it to completion.

choices.text: Oxidize phenol with chromic acid to install the ester
choices.feedback: Oxidation changes oxidation level, it does not form an ester linkage. Ester formation is a nucleophilic acyl substitution, not a redox step.

scenarios.debrief:
Structure elucidation has a fixed order and following it keeps you out of trouble. Calculate degrees of unsaturation from the formula, use IR to name the functional group, use NMR shift, integration and splitting to locate the pieces, then assemble a structure that accounts for every atom in the formula. If your proposed structure has the wrong molecular formula, it is wrong no matter how well it fits the spectra.

The shift difference that decided this problem is worth memorizing: a methyl bonded to a carbonyl carbon sits near 2.1 to 2.3 ppm, while a methyl bonded to an ester oxygen sits near 3.7 to 4.0 ppm. That single number distinguishes phenyl acetate from methyl benzoate.

> **Key:** In synthesis you may always convert a more reactive acid derivative into a less reactive one. Acid chloride and anhydride acylate alcohols and amines readily; esters and amides do not acylate anything without harsh conditions or enzymes.

> **On the exam:** The acetyl-transfer step you just used is the same chemistry as aspirin manufacture and the same chemistry by which aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase in the body.
